Full teaching text Risk analysis and scenario development with FIVER FIVER is a recurring process of framing and understanding, identifying, evaluating, revising and responding. Learning, trust-building and expectation management remain active throughout the cycle. Frame and understand Precaution begins with early situational awareness. Organisations should systematically gather information from professional environments, communities, media and relevant experts. Stakeholder mapping and attention to weak signals can make emerging problems visible before they escalate. Identify The organisation identifies concrete problems and contested issues that may develop into risks or crises. It must separate relevant signals from noise, prioritise matters requiring action and avoid dismissing unclear issues merely because their consequences remain uncertain. Evaluate Each identified matter is assessed in relation to possible consequences, uncertainty, vulnerability and organisational capacity. Probability and consequence may inform the assessment, but cannot replace judgement. Scenarios help decision-makers examine plausible developments, demanding conditions and necessary preparedness. Revise Analysis must lead to practical change. Organisations may need to revise preparedness plans, roles, resources, routines, coordination or policy. Communication cannot compensate for a material or organisational problem that remains unchanged. Respond Response requires defined roles, rapid notification, coordinated information and honest communication about decisions and uncertainty. Stakeholder involvement continues before, during and after the event. Evaluation turns experience into revised procedures and begins the cycle again. FIVER was developed and revised through teaching at Volda University College, NTNU and HAW Kiel, work with crisis exercises, and research on municipal preparedness. Pedagogical use does not constitute a claim of empirical validation. text: Media distortion, news framing and mediatization | MMP311 Media distortion, news framing and mediatization The original concept of media distortion Media distortion 2.0 News framing and the construction of meaning Frames in the communication process Generic frames and methodological precision From framing to mediatization The integrated contribution to analysis work in issue and risk management References Media distortion, news framing and mediatization | MMP311 Skip to main content V INFBV Skills Subjects Knowledge Search MMP311 Learning path Models Cases Full texts Glossary MMP311 / Full-text explanations / Media distortion, news framing and mediatization Media distortion, news framing and mediatization MMP311 · Version 1.0 · Revised 19th of November, 2026 by Kristian Fuglseth (opens in a new tab) Issue, risk and crisis analysis often begins before a situation has acquired a stable definition. An event, complaint, policy proposal or public controversy may constitute an issue for one actor, a problem for another and a possible risk for a third. Analysis must therefore examine how the situation becomes relevant, which consequences are made visible, which values organise disagreement and which actors acquire the authority to define what the situation concerns. News media constitute one part of the environment under analysis. Their significance does not lie only in disseminating information. Journalistic selection and presentation affect which aspects of a situation become publicly visible, how actors and consequences are connected, and which definitions appear credible or actionable. Public communication may therefore influence the conditions under which organisations detect issues, assess problems and risks, and decide whether a response requires communication, organisational change or both. Media distortion, news framing and mediatization describe different levels of this process. Media distortion identifies techniques used to select and present information. Framing concerns how selected elements are organised into interpretations of problems, causes, responsibilities and possible responses. Mediatization concerns longer-term changes in the relationships between media and other institutions. Maintaining these distinctions makes it possible to move from close analysis of a particular text to an assessment of public relevance and, where the material permits it, institutional change. The original concept of media distortion Hernes first developed the concept of medievri in the 1970s. The original argument addressed the transition from an information-poor to an information-rich society. The institutional question was how media altered the internal functioning of other social units and the relationships among them (Hernes, 1977, p. 181). In the information-rich society, abundance created a shortage of attention and assessment time. Selection and presentation consequently became central. The original model identified sharpening, simplification, polarisation, intensification and concretisation. Sharpening makes a principal point more distinct. Simplification reduces complexity. Polarisation organises actors and positions through contrast. Intensification strengthens conflict or confrontation. Concretisation gives priority to observable events and examples over abstract relationships (Hernes, 1977, pp. 187–188). Personification was omitted from the original article and added later (Hernes, 2019, p. 30). These techniques do not necessarily indicate factual error, deliberate manipulation or poor journalism. Hernes tied them to limited capacity, assumptions about normal knowledge, democratic accessibility and the need to attract an audience (Hernes, 1977, p. 188). The analytical task is therefore to show what each operation does in the material. Sharpening may clarify an issue while narrowing the range of relevant interpretations. Concretisation may make an abstract risk understandable through a particular case while obscuring structural conditions. Personification may make responsibility visible while directing attention away from organisational routines or institutional relationships. The techniques are methodologically relevant in analysis work in issue and risk management because they help separate the underlying matter from its mediated presentation. They provide concrete questions for close reading. What has been sharpened? What complexity has been removed? Which actors or positions are organised as opposites? Which example is made representative? Which institutional process is presented through an individual? Media distortion 2.0 Hernes (2019) revisits the original model from a media environment that differs structurally from the system in which it was developed. The 2019 article first reconstructs the transition to information abundance and restates the original techniques (Hernes, 2019, p. 14). It then traces the fragmentation of the newspaper-industrial complex, digital convergence, continuous news flows, personalised distribution and the movement from one-to-many communication towards interactive all-to-all communication (Hernes, 2019, pp. 21–27). The revision is therefore more extensive than an update to a list of presentational techniques. Professional news organisations no longer exercise the same degree of control over access to mass publicity. Digital platforms allow political actors, organisations and users to publish, distribute and amplify material directly. Selection still occurs, but it is distributed across editorial routines, platform structures, strategic actors and audience activity. Hernes develops the argument through conflict and emotionalisation. Information enters an existing field of tensions rather than a social vacuum, and new issues can reactivate established front lines and group identities (Hernes, 2019, p. 28). Circulation is not neutral distribution. People can mobilise, warn, endorse and oppose in real time. Hernes captures this affective potential in the formulation “When we care, we share” (Hernes, 2019, p. 28). The next step concerns conflict organisation. A new matter can function as a loyalty test and activate latent conflicts. How the conflict is defined affects who becomes involved, what the dispute concerns and how strongly the parties mobilise (Hernes, 2019, p. 29). A single event may become a multi-issue that divides opinion in several ways and mobilises different publics for different reasons. Hernes’s conflict thesis is that an information-rich society contains not only a struggle for attention, but also competition over issues capable of activating latent conflicts (Hernes, 2019, p. 29). Media distortion 2.0 thus extends the original model from journalistic presentation towards the broader organisation of attention, circulation and conflict. The original techniques remain relevant, but they operate in a changed infrastructure. Sharpening and polarisation can be performed by news organisations, political actors, organisations and users. Intensification may occur through repeated circulation, commentary and platform interaction. Personification may connect a structural issue to one individual whose actions become a focal point for wider conflicts. This development is directly relevant to environmental assessment. Organisations may first encounter an emerging issue through fragmented signals distributed across news media, social platforms, stakeholder communication and political debate. High visibility does not in itself document material severity. Extensive circulation may reflect emotional mobilisation, strategic amplification or the activation of an established conflict. Conversely, an issue with limited media visibility may still represent a substantial organisational problem or risk. News framing and the construction of meaning Entman (1993) places selection within a wider process of meaning-making. Framing involves selecting aspects of perceived reality and making them more salient in communication. A frame may support a problem definition, a causal interpretation, a moral evaluation and a proposed response (Entman, 1993, p. 52). Framing is consequently more than choosing a topic or angle. It concerns how several elements are organised into an interpretation of what has happened, why the situation matters and what should follow. A frame cannot be established from one word, source or isolated feature. Beyer (2010) describes frames as constructions that emphasise certain aspects while connecting the selection to definitions, causes, consequences and evaluations (Beyer, 2010, p. 163). The analytical object is the relationship among the elements. A reference to disagreement does not by itself establish a conflict frame. The analysis must show how disagreement structures the presentation and connects actors, causes, values and possible outcomes. Framing overlaps with agenda-setting without becoming identical to it. First-level agenda-setting concerns the relative prominence of issues. Second-level agenda-setting concerns the prominence of attributes connected to issues or actors. Framing places greater emphasis on relationships among elements and on the construction of causes, evaluations and meaning. Beyer (2010) places framing, agenda-setting and priming in the same theoretical discussion without subsuming them under one conceptual framework (Beyer, 2010, p. 164). The distinction clarifies the role of news values in environmental assessment. Timeliness, conflict, proximity, consequence, personalisation and continuity may help explain why a matter attracts journalistic attention. These criteria do not document stakeholder attitudes or public opinion. Nor do they determine whether the matter constitutes an issue, problem or risk. They provide indicators of possible public relevance. Framing analysis then examines how selected elements organise this relevance into a particular account. Frames in the communication process Beyer (2010) distinguishes strategic frames, journalistic frames, news or media frames, and framing effects (Beyer, 2010, p. 165). Strategic frames are promoted by actors who seek to define a matter before or during journalistic processing. Journalistic frames guide selection and construction in news work. News frames are observable in published content. Framing effects concern the encounter between the mediated account and its audiences. The distinction defines what different materials can document. A content analysis can identify patterns in published news but cannot by itself establish a journalist’s intention. A news report containing an organisation’s definition does not prove that the organisation successfully controlled the frame. A textual frame does not document how a public interpreted the matter. Beyer (2010) associates interviews, observation and document analysis with the study of strategic and journalistic framing, while frames in published content can be examined through content analysis (Beyer, 2010, p. 165). Audience responses require reception-oriented material. Framing research may investigate cognitive, attitudinal and behavioural responses, but these effects cannot be inferred from the media text alone (Beyer, 2010, p. 166). Knudsen (2016) expresses the same methodological separation by treating news frames as both dependent and independent variables. As a dependent variable, a frame is something to be explained through actors, routines, events and institutional conditions. As an independent variable, it is examined as a possible influence on how audiences, organisations or decision-makers interpret an issue (Knudsen, 2016, p. 10). Environmental assessment draws on forms of material that must not be treated as equivalent. Media texts document public representations. Stakeholder documents and statements document articulated positions. Interviews may provide access to experiences and interpretations. Surveys can document distributions of attitudes within a defined population. Organisational records may document decisions and changes in practice. Each source supports different conclusions. Generic frames and methodological precision Beyer (2010) distinguishes issue-specific frames from generic frames. Issue-specific frames organise the interpretation of a particular matter. Generic frames may occur across policy areas, periods and media systems. Conflict, personalisation, human interest, responsibility and game or strategy are examples of generic structures. The distinction affects research design because issue-specific frames are often developed inductively, whereas generic frames are commonly examined deductively (Beyer, 2010, p. 165). Coding only the dominant frame creates a problem. A news report may contain conflict, substantive policy discussion, personalisation and strategic interpretation in different degrees. Requiring the analyst to select one dominant category removes information about how the frames coexist. Beyer argues that broad, holistic categories also weaken conceptual validity because they do not show which features led the coder to identify the frame (Beyer, 2010, p. 167). Each generic frame should therefore be operationalised through several concrete questions. In an analysis of conflict framing, one variable may assess whether the report presents disagreement among parties, individuals, groups or countries. The variables connect an abstract concept to observable textual features (Beyer, 2010, p. 168). The variables may be coded through graded scales rather than a binary distinction between presence and absence. A graded scale can distinguish among no presence, limited presence, substantial presence and principal focus. This procedure retains more information about partly latent textual properties (Beyer, 2010, p. 169). It also permits several frames to occur in the same unit. Beyer’s empirical example shows that game, issue, personalisation and conflict frames can coexist and correlate in different ways (Beyer, 2010, p. 174). These principles remain relevant in qualitative analysis. A frame should be reconstructed from several observations. The analyst should state which features support the interpretation, consider competing frames and avoid presenting latent meaning as self-evident. If systematic coding is used, the scale, codebook and reliability procedure must be documented. From framing to mediatization Hjarvard (2016) defines mediatization as a process in which relationships between media and other social and cultural domains change and create altered conditions for communication and interaction (Hjarvard, 2016, p. 39). The concept moves the analysis from particular messages to institutional relationships and change over time. Mediation and mediatization must remain distinct. Mediation concerns communication through a medium. Mediatization concerns longer-term changes in communicative conditions and institutional practices. A political statement on a digital platform is an instance of mediation. Evidence that political organisations have changed routines, staffing, timing or decision-making in anticipation of media formats may support a mediatization argument. Knudsen (2016) connects framing to this institutional level. Frames can be studied both as outcomes of journalistic, strategic and institutional conditions and as possible influences on publics, decision-makers and organisations (Knudsen, 2016, p. 10). The relationship is not one-directional. Political and organisational actors promote frames, manage access to information and attempt to influence journalistic definitions. News organisations select, modify or contest these strategic frames (Knudsen, 2016, p. 12). Media logic provides a possible meeting point. Frames belong to its aesthetic dimension because they concern recurrent forms of presentation, dramaturgy and emphasis. They also acquire an institutional dimension when stable relations among media organisations, professional routines and preferred sources reproduce characteristic accounts of issues and actors (Knudsen, 2016, p. 12). The development from the original medievri to media distortion 2.0 makes this institutional connection more visible. The original model identifies techniques through which editorial media format information. The revised model addresses an environment where these operations are distributed among more actors and infrastructures. Framing explains how selected elements form interpretations. Mediatization asks whether recurring conditions of selection, circulation and framing contribute to changes in organisational practice. The concepts do not form a deterministic sequence. A presentational technique does not automatically produce one frame. A frame does not guarantee an audience response. Repeated circulation does not by itself establish institutional change. Knudsen concludes that framing research alone may fail to explain how media influence reaches the institutional level, while mediatization research alone may fail to identify the communicative mechanisms through which influence develops (Knudsen, 2016, p. 16). The integrated contribution to analysis work in issue and risk management The theoretical development supports a layered approach to environmental assessment. The first layer concerns the underlying matter. What has occurred? Which evidence is available? What remains uncertain? Which possible consequences follow from the documented conditions? The second layer concerns relevance. Who has made the matter visible? Which publics recognise a consequence or shared concern? Which values organise their interpretations? News values may indicate why the matter attracts attention, but they do not measure the seriousness of the issue or the distribution of public attitudes. The third layer concerns presentation and framing. Which elements have been selected? Which techniques shape the presentation? How are the problem, causes, responsibilities and possible responses organised? Which interpretations are made prominent, and which alternatives disappear from view? The fourth layer concerns circulation and conflict organisation. Does the matter activate established oppositions? Does emotional mobilisation amplify the issue? Does the same event function as a multi-issue for publics organised around different values? The fifth layer concerns organisational interpretation. Has the organisation treated visibility as evidence of material risk? Has it recognised the relevant publics? Does its first analysis reproduce the dominant frame? Which additional evidence is needed before the matter can be categorised as an organisational problem or risk? The sixth layer concerns institutional adaptation. Has the organisation changed routines or priorities because it anticipates recurring media formats and expectations? Is the observed change temporary and case-specific, or does it indicate a longer-term alteration in communicative conditions? PRK, SOFT and FIVER organise different parts of this work. PRK provides categories for examining how a matter is defined and how it may move conditionally among issue, problem, risk and crisis. SOFT tests the social and organisational assumptions underlying the situation analysis. FIVER connects interpretation to evaluation, organisational change and response. Media distortion, framing and mediatization do not replace these models. They provide theory and method for analysing the mediated environment in which the models are applied. This integration preserves a necessary boundary. Media analysis can identify representations, visibility and framing. Stakeholder analysis can document articulated interests and positions. Reception material can document interpretations and attitudes. Risk assessment can evaluate possible outcomes and uncertainty. Organisational analysis can document decisions and institutional change. text: Glossary | MMP311 Glossary Glossary | MMP311 Skip to main content V INFBV Skills Subjects Knowledge Search MMP311 Learning path Models Cases Full texts Glossary MMP311 / Glossary Glossary Core concepts used across issue, risk and crisis analysis. Issue A matter becomes an issue when an actor makes conduct, consequences, values or responsibility relevant before the organisation has established that a problem exists. Problem A documented condition that obstructs valued outcomes or creates an expectation gap requiring investigation, clarification or change. Risk Possible future consequences considered together with uncertainty, exposure, vulnerability and what actors value. Crisis A situation that threatens valued outcomes, compresses decision time and challenges ordinary organisational capacity. Public A group that forms around a recognised consequence, shared concern or contested value. A public is not identical to a predefined target group. Framing Selection and organisation of elements into an interpretation of a problem, causes, evaluations and possible responses. Media distortion Presentational operations such as sharpening, simplification, polarisation, intensification, concretisation and personification. Mediatization Longer-term changes in relationships between media and other institutions that alter communicative conditions and organisational practices. PRK An analytical model for conditional movement among problem, risk and crisis. The model does not assume automatic escalation. SOFT A reflexive model for testing social and organisational assumptions, missing publics and blind spots in a situation analysis. FIVER A five-stage framework for understanding, identifying, evaluating, changing and responding to issues, possible problems and risks. Journalistic attention News criteria News criteria help explain why some issues receive attention while others remain less visible. They are editorial assessment tools, not neutral measures of social importance. 1. Significance The story is relevant and important to a substantial audience. Events affecting many people normally receive greater priority. 2. Identification The story gives audiences people, groups or situations with which they can identify. Explain manufactured, de-bounded and unequally distributed risk. Use non-knowledge and unknown unknowns in a case analysis. Identify who decides and who carries possible consequences. Risk is not simply a measurable property of a hazard. It is also a way of anticipating possible harm under conditions of incomplete knowledge, disagreement and unequal exposure. Hazard, risk, uncertainty and ambiguity Hazard A potential source of harm. Risk A possible development considered in relation to valued outcomes, decisions and consequences. Uncertainty Limits to what is known about probability, consequences, causal relations or future development. Ambiguity Disagreement about meaning, values, responsibility or acceptable action, even when actors share some of the same factual information. Read for Beck: de-bounding, anticipation and world risk society. Sørensen: calculability, non-knowledge and constructivist realism. Source basis. Sørensen shows that Beck’s risk concept is not equivalent to conventional calculable risk. Beck’s “new risks” combine manufactured origins with qualities associated with hazards: they may be difficult to calculate, insure, delimit and observe directly (Sørensen, 2018, pp. 6–12). First and second modernity In first modernity, industrial institutions treated uncertainty as something that could increasingly be measured, insured and controlled. Beck’s second or reflexive modernity describes a condition in which modernisation confronts the side effects of its own success. Scientific and technological development remains necessary, but also produces hazards, dependencies and non-knowledge that established institutions struggle to contain (Sørensen, 2018, pp. 7–9). Manufactured and de-bounded risks Beck’s world risk society is not defined by a simple increase in everyday danger. It is defined by risks that cross spatial, temporal and social boundaries. Beck uses ecological, financial and terrorist risks to show how consequences escape national control, unfold over long periods and make causal responsibility difficult to assign (Beck, 2002, pp. 40–45). These risks are unequally distributed. Their transnational reach does not mean that all groups or regions are exposed in the same way. Decisions and benefits may be concentrated in one place while consequences are carried elsewhere (Beck, 2002, pp. 41–42; Sørensen, 2018, pp. 13–15). Invisibility and non-knowledge Many modern risks cannot be perceived directly. Radiation, climate change and toxic exposure become visible through scientific theories, instruments and institutional practices. Sørensen describes this through Beck’s idea of “second-hand non-experience”: citizens depend on expertise to identify risks while scientific disagreement can increase rather than remove uncertainty (Sørensen, 2018, pp. 7–10). Beck distinguishes what is not yet known from “unknown unknowns”: knowledge whose absence is itself unknown when decisions are made. Risk communication must therefore explain both the evidence and the limits of present knowledge. Organised irresponsibility and unequal consequences When harm results from many lawful and distributed decisions, no single actor may appear responsible. Beck’s wider work describes this institutional diffusion as organised irresponsibility. The concept is analytically useful, but it should not be used as a substitute for tracing concrete authority, decisions, benefits and exposure in a particular case. Worked example CFC gases were introduced before their effect on the ozone layer was understood. The case shows how decisions can create consequences that were unknown at the time, and how scientific knowledge can later make an invisible risk actionable. Student activity Use a public risk assessment and three news reports about the same case. Identify the hazard, the assessed risks, explicit uncertainty, possible unknown unknowns and competing value judgements. Then state who makes decisions and who carries the possible consequences. Common misunderstanding Risk society does not mean that everyday life is simply becoming more dangerous. The concept concerns how modernisation produces risks that may be difficult to calculate, delimit, insure and observe directly. Identify care, consensus and crisis communication. Assess whether trust is warranted by competence, integrity and conduct. Use SOFT to identify social and organisational blind spots. Risk communication connects assessment, public interpretation, values and practical action. It cannot be reduced to transferring expert information to a passive audience. Assessment, perception and communication Risk assessment evaluates possible harm, uncertainty and vulnerability. Risk perception concerns how actors interpret relevance, credibility, fairness and control. Risk communication is the exchange through which knowledge, uncertainty, values and possible action are made available for scrutiny and decision. Three communication situations Care communication Supports informed choices and protective action where the hazard is reasonably established. Consensus communication Addresses disagreement about decisions, values, distribution and acceptable risk. Crisis communication Supports urgent action and coordination under time pressure, uncertainty and possible harm. The situations may overlap. A crisis can contain long-standing value conflict, and care communication may fail when unequal resources make recommended action unrealistic. Expertise, ethos and warranted trust Expert knowledge enters a particular rhetorical situation. Audiences assess not only the information, but also the expert, the institution, previous conduct and the interests surrounding the claim. Trust should not be treated as an attitude that communication can manufacture. Communication supports warranted trust when competence, integrity, goodwill, uncertainty and institutional limitations are visible. Use SOFT to test the communication SOFT asks whether the communication accounts for social conditions, opinions and expectations, framing, transparency and organisational conditions. The lens helps distinguish an information deficit from a conflict about values, unequal consequences or organisational conduct. Worked example A drinking-water warning combines crisis communication with care communication. Residents need immediate protective advice, but the authority must also explain uncertainty, unequal access to alternatives and when new information will be available. Student activity Compare an expert message and a public response concerning the same risk. Identify what each treats as evidence, which uncertainty is acknowledged, which values are contested, and which recommendations assume resources that some audiences may not have. Common misunderstanding Being open about uncertainty is not the same as being vague. Useful uncertainty communication states what is known, what is not known, why the limitation matters and what will happen next. Expected output A short risk message containing known evidence, explicit uncertainty, recommended action, justification and an accessibility check. Check your understanding What separates risk perception from risk assessment? When does consensus communication become necessary? Why can communication not manufacture warranted trust? Identify who makes a matter relevant and on what grounds. Separate investigation and adaptation from organisational defence. Analyse how journalistic techniques affect visibility. An issue begins when an actor makes a matter relevant by questioning conduct, consequences, values or responsibility. Early issues management examines the claim before the organisation defines the matter as a problem. Issue before problem An issue may be clarified, accommodated or resolved before it produces a problem. It becomes a problem when it creates an expectation gap, obstructs legitimate goals, harms stakeholders or places the organisation under sustained pressure to act. Early work therefore asks who points to the issue, which experience or evidence supports the claim, and what the organisation can clarify or change. Possible responses include clarification, participation, adaptation, changes in policy or practice, and a reasoned rejection of a claim. Issues management is not organisational self-defence. It is a systematic way to test whether conduct, consequences, values or responsibility require action. How an issue becomes visible Hernes’s concept of media distortion ( medievridning ) identifies accentuation, simplification, polarisation, intensification, concretisation and personification as techniques that shape attention. These techniques do not automatically create the underlying problem. They affect what becomes visible, how responsibility is attributed and how quickly an organisation must respond. Worked example A local group questions a proposed service change. The issue exists when the claim is made relevant. It becomes an organisational problem only if the proposal creates an unresolved expectation gap, material harm or sustained conflict. Student activity Select an emerging issue. State what can still be clarified before it becomes a problem. Identify the conduct or non-response that could move the issue towards risk or crisis, and propose one preventive organisational change. Common misunderstanding Media attention documents visibility, not proof that the organisation caused the issue. The underlying claim, conduct and consequences require separate evidence. Expected output A one-page issue brief identifying the claim, evidence, stakeholders, expectation gap, clarification needs and possible organisational change. Recognise new issues, problems and risks created by crisis response. Use SOFT to identify blind spots in a situation analysis. Distinguish media distortion, framing, media logic and mediatization. PRK locates conditional movement between problem, risk and crisis. SOFT challenges what the first situation analysis has made visible. Issue detection before PRK An issue stands before the PRK triad. It may be clarified without becoming a problem. If the matter exposes an expectation gap, material harm or sustained conflict, it may reveal or produce a problem. A problem may create risk without becoming a crisis, while crisis response may create new problems and risks. Issue A matter made relevant by an actor Clarified or handled Dialogue, adaptation or reasoned rejection Problem Expectation gap, harm or sustained pressure Problem ↔ Risk ↔ Crisis ↺ learning and new issues Figure 1. Issue detection precedes PRK. Movement is conditional and reversible, not an inevitable escalation. SOFT as a critical lens The resource uses SOFT as the name of a teaching lens rather than as a strict letter-by-letter initialism. It tests social conditions, opinions and expectations, framing, transparency and organisational conditions. The lens asks whose exposure and knowledge are visible, which interpretation dominates, what the organisation can explain, and whether it has authority and capacity to change. Media distortion, framing, media logic and mediatization These concepts operate at different analytical levels. Media distortion concerns concrete presentation techniques. Framing concerns selection, problem definition, causal interpretation, responsibility and remedies. Media logic concerns technological, aesthetic and institutional working conditions. Mediatization concerns longer-term changes in the relationship between media and other institutions. The levels can be connected analytically, but they do not constitute a single documented causal chain. Worked example A technical disruption may be handled without public controversy. If service users experience unequal consequences, the disruption becomes a problem. Poor response may create legitimacy risk, while an acute operational breakdown may become a crisis and generate new issues. SOFT worksheet Table 1. Five fields for challenging the first situation analysis. Field Question Evidence What may be missing? Social conditions Who is exposed, excluded or dependent? Opinions and expectations What do stakeholders consider legitimate or safe? Framing How are cause, responsibility and remedies defined? Transparency What is known, unknown, withheld or difficult to explain? Organisational conditions What authority, resources and capacity for change exist? Then identify what the first account misses because of social position, framing, transparency or organisational limits. This English resource adapts Kristian Fuglseth (opens in a new tab) ’s Norwegian teaching text used with students at NTNU and HAW Kiel. Learning outcomes Use the five FIVER phases and fifteen work tasks. Separate strategic aims from tactical tasks. Identify organisational change before proposing communication measures. Plan evaluation and institutional learning. FIVER retains its Norwegian acronym: F orstå (frame and understand), I dentifisere (identify), V urdere (evaluate), E ndre (change) and R espondere (respond). It is a five-stage framework for understanding and handling issues, possible problems and risks before they develop into crises. Trust-building, expectation management and learning remain strategic aims throughout the process. 1. Frame and understand Map stakeholders and expectations, analyse drivers and the media environment, and establish structures for information and communication. The first stage should include communication, empathy, cooperation and cultural understanding, because these conditions affect whether the organisation is perceived as credible and responsible. Map stakeholders and their expectations. Analyse drivers, public debate and the media environment. Build structures and plans, using SOFT, FMECA, PSO or another suitable system. 2. Identify Identify issues that may develop into problems. Clarify expectation gaps, distinguish relevant signals from noise, and prioritise matters according to their possible consequences and need for follow-up. Clarify expectation gaps. Distinguish noise from relevant risk signals. Prioritise and rank issues. 3. Evaluate Assess probability, consequences, uncertainty and vulnerability. Locate causes and responsibility, examine gaps between stakeholder expectations and organisational practice, and test whether the matter has been framed too narrowly. The analysis must also establish whether the problem is communicative, organisational, financial, technical or operational. Analyse probability and consequence without treating the matrix as the whole assessment. Locate causes, responsibility and missing redundancy. Critically reassess the problem definition and examine expectation gaps. Reframing is not positive spin. 4. Change Move from analysis to action. Choose a reactive, adaptive, proactive, initiative-taking or interactive strategy. Revise plans, resources, routines, roles and organisational structures. Distinguish material, organisational, strategic and communicative change. Adjusting the narrative cannot replace material or organisational change. Select a strategy suited to the issue and the organisation. Adapt plans, resources and measures. Revise communication, roles or structures where necessary. 5. Respond Put decisions into practice. Communication must correspond with action, coordination must include relevant stakeholders and partners, and evaluation must occur during as well as after the response. Learning becomes institutional only when it changes plans, exercises, routines and culture. Act and communicate clearly. Coordinate and evaluate while the response develops. Institutionalise learning and improvement. Worked example A municipality receives repeated concerns about preparedness for a service interruption. FIVER starts by mapping stakeholders and expectations, not by drafting a message. The process must identify what plans, resources or roles should change before communication is selected. The group must identify at least one organisational change before proposing communication measures, and must state how learning will be assigned, documented and followed up. Common misunderstanding Reframing is not positive spin. It is a critical reassessment of the problem definition, relevant evidence, responsibility and possible response. Expected output A completed FIVER workshop record with evidence, decisions, responsibility, deadlines and evaluation criteria. Suggested citation for the framework. Fuglseth, K. (2025). FIVER: A five-stage framework for issues analysis and response [Teaching and analytical framework]. Check your understanding Why does FIVER retain a Norwegian acronym? What must be produced before the response phase? How does learning become institutional rather than temporary? Full-text explanation. The full-text explanation shows how environmental assessment can distinguish evidence, visibility, framing and organisational adaptation. Read media distortion, news framing and mediatization . This resource reorganises and expands selected arguments from the crisis communication chapter in Brataas, Bakken, and Fuglseth (2026), Etterpåklok på forhånd . It is not a reproduction of the published chapter. Learning outcomes Distinguish crisis information from crisis communication. Plan internal and external communication as connected work. Write an initial update under uncertainty. Prioritise stakeholders, channels and fallback channels. Evaluate communication as part of crisis management. Crisis communication is part of crisis management. Information affects safety, coordination, legitimacy and the organisation’s capacity to act. Crisis information and crisis communication Crisis information distributes verified facts and instructions. Crisis communication is broader: it connects decision-making, listening, coordination, interpretation, uncertainty and relations with affected groups. Internal communication must begin before or alongside external communication because employees, leaders and operational teams need a shared basis for action. Before, during and after Before a crisis, the organisation maps scenarios, stakeholders, responsibilities, channels and fallback systems, and practises difficult decisions. During a crisis, it should communicate what is known, what is not known, what is being done, what people should do and when the next update will come. After the acute phase, communication supports explanation, accountability, learning and long-term relations. Principles under pressure Speed, clarity, openness and responsibility are practical demands, not slogans. Speed without verification can cause harm. Openness has legal and ethical limits. Clarity must not conceal uncertainty. Responsibility requires visible decisions, correction and follow-up, not merely a visible spokesperson. Media, news criteria and framing News values help explain attention, not social importance. Significance, identification, sensation, timeliness, conflict, elite actors, proximity and exclusivity shape selection. Hernes’s media distortion and framing theory help analyse how crisis coverage sharpens, simplifies, personalises and attributes responsibility. Organisations cannot control this process through message discipline alone. Plans, stakeholders and alternative channels A crisis communication plan should connect principles with roles, mobilisation, situational awareness, internal communication, external communication, monitoring, technology, templates and evaluation. Alternative channels are required for loss of power, networks and internal systems. Plans must account for language, disability, unequal access and the needs of directly affected groups. Exercises and learning Exercises should test incomplete information, media pressure, internal needs, affected stakeholders, social media traffic, inter-organisational coordination and technological failure. Evaluation should separate learning from blame and assign responsibility for actual change. Stakeholder map Table 1. Minimum stakeholder mapping for crisis communication. Stakeholder Information and action needs Relationship and channel Responsible function Directly affected groups Safety, assistance, uncertainty and next update Direct, accessible and two-way communication Named operational owner Employees and leaders Shared situation, decisions, roles and support Internal primary and fallback channels Management and internal communication Partners and responders Coordination, authority and resource needs Established liaison channels Coordination lead Media and wider publics Verified facts, accountability and protective advice Briefings, website and monitored channels Spokesperson and communication team Minimum crisis communication plan Mandate and principles. Roles, authority and mobilisation thresholds. Situational awareness and verification. Internal communication. External stakeholders and accessibility. Channel priorities and fallback channels. Media relations and social media monitoring. Templates, logging and approval. Evaluation and assigned follow-up. AI-supported work AI may support transcription, translation, monitoring and drafting, but output requires human verification. Crisis use must protect personal data, sensitive operational information and information security. Synthetic images, automated spokespersons and unverified summaries can undermine both accuracy and accountability. Worked example A service interruption begins with incomplete information. The first update should identify the verified disruption, name what remains unknown, state protective action, assign responsibility and provide the time of the next update. Two initial updates Useful initial update We are investigating a disruption affecting the municipal water supply in the eastern service area. The cause and duration are not yet confirmed. Residents in the affected streets should not use tap water for drinking or food preparation until further notice. Bottled water is available at the community centre from 14:00. The municipality will publish the next update by 15:30, even if the situation has not changed. The update separates verified information from uncertainty, gives protective action, identifies support and commits to a next update. Poor initial update We are aware of a situation and have everything under control. More information will follow. The message provides no scope, evidence, action, accountability or time for the next update. “Under control” is an unsupported reassurance. Student activity Draft the first public update for a developing crisis. Include one verified fact, one explicit uncertainty, one protective action, one accountability statement and the time of the next update. Common misunderstanding Speed does not justify unverified information. Openness does not require disclosure of protected personal data or sensitive operational information. Expected output An initial public update, an internal situation note, a stakeholder map, a fallback-channel plan and two evaluation criteria. Full reference to the original source. Distinguish material, method, analysis and discussion. Use theory as an analytical tool rather than decoration. Separate documentation, interpretation and uncertainty. Use sources and AI in an auditable way. Academic writing makes the analytical movement visible. A strong text connects a precise question, defined material, a transparent method, concepts that change what can be seen, and conclusions that do not exceed the evidence. Begin with a question the material can answer A research question should identify the phenomenon, the analytical purpose and an empirical boundary. “How do Norwegian authorities communicate risk?” is too broad. “How is uncertainty framed in two public preparedness campaigns published between 2024 and 2026?” identifies both material and analytical focus. Three useful forms Theoretical essay Develop and test a conceptual argument through precise engagement with research. The essay still needs a question, an explicit selection of literature and a bounded conclusion. Case analysis Define the case, material and method. Use PRK, SOFT or FIVER only when the framework changes what the analysis can identify. A model is not evidence. Evaluation of communication practice State criteria before assessing performance. Separate what the communication contains, how it can reasonably be interpreted and what cannot be concluded without audience or outcome data. Move from evidence to interpretation A useful paragraph establishes a claim, presents observable evidence, explains the relationship and ends with a bounded interpretation. Quotations, screenshots, documents and examples must demonstrate the claim rather than decorate the text. Make theory do analytical work Define the concept, identify the relevant feature in the material, explain how the concept changes the interpretation, and state the limit of the inference. If a theory can be removed without changing the analysis, it is not doing analytical work. Distinguish material, method, analysis and discussion The material is what is studied. The method explains how it is selected and analysed. The analysis shows patterns and examples. The discussion relates findings to theory, previous research and alternative explanations. These functions may appear in different structures; IMRaD is not mandatory for every assignment. Use generative AI without outsourcing responsibility AI can support outlining, language revision and comparison of formulations. The student remains responsible for source retrieval, quotation accuracy, references, analytical decisions and the submitted text. Never cite a source that has not been opened and checked. Document AI use according to the course and institutional rules. Worked example Observation: A preparedness campaign repeatedly uses household images and imperative verbs. Evidence: Three posts show stored water, batteries and food alongside “You must be prepared”. Explanation: SOFT directs attention to framing and unequal household capacity. Interpretation: The campaign individualises preparedness, but the material alone cannot establish how audiences respond. Paraphrase, quotation and secondary sources A paraphrase restates a source in a new formulation while preserving its meaning and citing the source. A direct quotation reproduces the wording exactly and requires quotation marks and a page number where available. A secondary citation should be used sparingly and must make clear that the original work was not consulted directly. Prefer a DOI for scholarly publications and a stable institutional URL for web sources. Avoid overinterpretation A textual pattern does not document an actor’s motive. Two simultaneous developments do not establish causation. A rhetorical analysis does not establish audience effects without audience data. A model organises analysis; it is not empirical evidence. Before submission The research question matches the material and method. Every quotation and reference has been checked in the original source. Findings and interpretation are explicitly distinguished. Alternative explanations and limits are stated. Tables and figures have numbers, captions, sources and text alternatives. AI use is documented according to the current HVO rule. [Check current institutional rule before publication.] Writing resources. Writing and referencing (opens in a new tab) , Volda University College; Toolkit for students (opens in a new tab) , Search & Write (sist sett 19.11.2026). Worked example: Framing household preparedness Examples of supplies for one week of household preparedness. Source: Norwegian Directorate for Civil Protection (DSB), How you can play your part in Norway’s emergency preparedness (opens in a new tab) (last accessed 19 November 2026). DSB visualises emergency preparedness through familiar household objects: water, food, batteries, lighting, medicines and hygiene products. The image translates preparedness from an abstract societal concern into practical tasks that households can carry out. The brochure recommends that households should be able to manage for one week. DSB connects this advice to collective preparedness: when more households manage without assistance, municipalities and emergency services can prioritise those who need help most. The material therefore frames preparedness as both personal responsibility and support for public crisis management. A SOFT analysis also draws attention to what the image leaves out. Households differ in income, storage space, health and access to social networks. The material supports an analysis of framing, but it does not document how audiences understand or act on the advice. Before and after revision Before The campaign clearly manipulates the audience by using fear, which proves that the authorities want people to obey. After The campaign combines imperative verbs with images of household supplies in three posts. These textual choices frame preparedness as an individual household responsibility. The material supports an interpretation of responsibilisation, but it does not document the authorities’ motive or the audience effect. The revised paragraph identifies evidence, explains the analytical relation and limits the inference. Model paragraph Claim: State the analytical point. Evidence: Present a quotation, visual feature, document or observed pattern. Explanation: Show how the evidence supports the claim. Interpretation: Relate the finding to the analytical concept. Limitation: State what the material does not establish. Student activity Revise one paragraph so that it moves from claim to evidence, explanation and bounded interpretation. Mark separately what the material documents, what you interpret and what remains uncertain. Common misunderstanding A textual pattern does not document motive. Simultaneous developments do not establish causation. Rhetorical analysis does not establish audience effects without audience data. Expected output A revised introduction containing a research question, material, method, analytical concepts, limitations and a source-checking plan. Writing as a process Academic writing rarely begins with a polished introduction. The video explains the logic of IMRaD. The story below offers a complementary way to think about drafting and revision. IMRaD , a video lecture from Lund University’s material on academic writing. The structure is useful when it fits the research task, but it is not mandatory for every assignment. Facsimile accompanying the writing reflection. The original sculpture is exhibited at the Galleria dell’Accademia in Florence. A writing reflection Finding your own David Michelangelo’s work offers a useful metaphor for academic writing. A first draft is not a finished sculpture. It is material that allows the writer to discover an argument, test connections and identify what the final text does not need. Read the full story Michelangelo wrote poems for people close to him, sometimes on the back of sketches or in the margins of letters. The writing did not have to begin as a finished public work. It could function as exploratory writing: a place where ideas developed before they had found their final form. The same principle applies to an academic assignment. Writer’s block often begins when the writer tries to polish sentences before enough material exists. Begin by examining what the assignment actually asks. Then write freely. Do not stop to correct every sentence or organise every paragraph. Writing is part of the thinking process. Begin with the raw block Use freewriting to bring possible claims, examples and questions onto the page. A mind map or a rough outline can then show how the ideas relate. You do not have to start with the introduction. Start where the material gives you something concrete to say. Rough out the argument Write a complete first draft before polishing transitions and individual words. If a word is missing, leave a marker and continue. Record page numbers while reading and taking notes. A later search for undocumented quotations and references consumes time and increases the risk of error. Remove what the text does not need Revision is not only correction. Each paragraph should explain, support or challenge the research question. Give the paragraph a clear analytical function, remove digressions and read difficult sentences aloud. Finally, check definitions, quotations, page numbers, references and the formal requirements for the assignment. The finished text does not appear in one inspired movement. It emerges through drafting, testing and removal. Read more about David David, disegno and the work of writing Imagine standing in front of a block of Carrara marble more than five metres tall. The stone is heavy, weathered and marked by earlier attempts to shape it. It has stood unused for decades. Now imagine that the block is not stone, but a blank page, a pile of research notes, several theories and a set of thoughts that have not yet found their form. Michelangelo’s David offers a way to think about what happens when we write. The comparison is not exact. Stone and language resist us in different ways. But both forms of work begin with material that contains more possibilities than the finished work can retain. Disegno and the search for form Michelangelo worked within a Renaissance understanding of disegno . The word can refer to drawing or design, but it also names the intellectual work through which an artist conceives and organises a form. A later tradition presents Michelangelo as an artist who released a figure already present in the marble. This idea should not be treated as a literal account of artistic creation. It nevertheless gives us a useful image of revision. Academic writing rarely begins with a pure argument waiting to be copied onto the page. The writer has to produce material before the argument becomes visible. Freewriting, notes, fragments and rough paragraphs create the block from which the text can be shaped. Revision then removes repetition, weak connections, unnecessary terminology and claims that the evidence cannot support. Clarity is not the decorative surface added at the end. It appears when the writer identifies what the argument is, what material supports it and what must be removed. Each deleted sentence and each more precise formulation can bring the underlying thought into clearer view. An unarmoured argument Michelangelo does not show David after the victory. Goliath is absent. The sculpture is commonly interpreted as presenting the moment before the confrontation. The sling is present, but understated. The body stands in contrapposto, with the weight distributed unevenly and the shoulders and hips turned in different directions. The pose combines stillness with the possibility of movement. This moment before action offers another image of academic work. A strong argument does not need to hide behind dense prose. It has to expose its assumptions, evidence and limits. Such openness makes the argument vulnerable to criticism, but it also makes scholarly examination possible. The point is not that academic writing should be stripped of theory or technical language. Precise concepts are necessary when they identify something that ordinary language cannot. The problem arises when terminology functions as armour. A concept must help the reader see the material differently. Otherwise, it protects the writer without strengthening the analysis. The gaze, the hand and the question The proportions of David have generated different explanations. The head and hands appear large in relation to parts of the body. One explanation connects these proportions to the sculpture’s original planned position high on Florence Cathedral, where some features would have needed to remain visible from below. The evidence does not settle every aspect of this interpretation. For a writer, however, the head, hand and gaze form a productive metaphor. Academic work joins perception to craft. The writer must identify a question, examine material and then give the analysis a form that other people can follow. Thinking and writing are not separate stages. The hand helps the mind discover what it is trying to say. The fixed gaze of David also matters. The opponent remains outside the sculpture, but the direction of attention makes the absent figure part of the scene. Academic questions work in a related way. A precise question directs attention towards something that is not yet explained. The writer does not defeat a difficult problem through volume or verbal force, but through selection, proportion and a well-aimed analytical claim. Il Gigante in the public square The marble block was known as il gigante , the giant. Michelangelo completed the sculpture between 1501 and 1504. The figure measures 5.17 metres and was originally commissioned for Florence Cathedral. A committee later decided that the finished work should stand beside the entrance to the Palazzo della Signoria, now known as Palazzo Vecchio. The placement changed how the sculpture could be understood. David, the smaller opponent who confronts Goliath, became associated with the civic freedom of the Florentine republic. This political meaning was not contained in the marble alone. It emerged through the biblical figure, the historical situation and the public place in which the sculpture stood. The original sculpture was moved to Galleria dell’Accademia in 1873 for conservation. A marble replica was installed at the former location in Piazza della Signoria in 1910. Visitors can therefore still encounter the figure in the civic setting that helped shape its political meaning, while the original stands inside the Galleria. Writing for a public Academic writing may begin privately in notes, sketches and provisional formulations. Its purpose is nevertheless public. The writer offers other people an argument that can be examined, challenged and developed. Moving a text into this public space requires more than polishing the language. The writer must show where the evidence comes from, distinguish observation from interpretation and state what the material cannot establish. This is where the image of carving reaches its limit. A scholarly argument is not a perfect figure that has always existed inside the material. The writer constructs it through choices. Other writers could organise the same material differently and reach other defensible interpretations. Revision does not uncover a single hidden truth. It makes the writer’s reasoning visible and accountable. The lasting value of the metaphor lies here. Begin with enough material. Look for the form that the material can sustain. Remove what obscures the argument. Keep the marks that show how the argument was made. Then allow the text to stand without unnecessary armour. The movement is circular rather than inevitable or linear. Use PRK in a case Compare the models What PRK helps you see Problem An organisational problem becomes visible when conduct, expectations or interpretations no longer align. Different stakeholders may disagree about both the problem and the appropriate response. Risk The issue represents risk when possible developments threaten people, values, operations, legitimacy or relationships. Assessment must include uncertainty and vulnerability, not only probability. Crisis A crisis places operations, decision-making or legitimacy under acute pressure. Crisis response can also expose older problems and produce new expectations. Problem Contested expectations and interpretations → Risk Possible harm, uncertainty and vulnerability → Crisis Acute pressure on operations or legitimacy Feedback: Crisis response and evaluation may reveal new problems and risks. Figure 1. The PRK framework. Problems, risks and crises can develop into one another; the movement is not necessarily linear. The accompanying text provides the full explanation. Use PRK in a case 01 Describe the matter What has happened, who is affected, and which expectations appear to be broken? 02 Locate the problem Is the core problem operational, organisational, communicative, political, or a combination? 03 Assess development Which values are at stake, what is uncertain, and what could make the situation more serious? 04 Consider crisis pressure Could established capacity, authority, trust or coordination become insufficient? 05 Feed learning back What must change in decisions, resources, routines or preparedness? Move to the next lens Challenge the situation analysis with SOFT Examine social conditions, public opinion, framing, transparency and organisational conditions. Open the SOFT approach → Organise the work with FIVER Turn the analysis into a recurring process from understanding and identification to revision and response. Open the FIVER model → Full teaching text Working strategically and tactically with PRK PRK separates strategic analysis from tactical communication while connecting problems, risks and crises across time. Before a crisis, organisations must work with emerging problems and possible risks. During a crisis, they must manage the underlying problem, changing risks and acute crisis communication at the same time. After the acute phase, unresolved problems may create new risks and secondary crises. Strategic level: Problem Organisations must continually scan their surroundings for matters that may become contested. The first task is to establish whether anyone experiences the matter as a problem. This provides the basis for identifying stakeholders, expectations and competing interpretations. Only then can the organisation assess whether the matter represents a risk and what forms of intervention may be required. Strategic work requires openness to weak signals and perspectives outside the organisation. No organisation operates in a vacuum. Unknown or neglected factors can become visible during an acute event and may develop into a secondary crisis. Strategic level: Risk When a contested matter may threaten people, services, values, legitimacy or relationships, it must enter the organisation's wider risk assessment. Analysis should examine stakeholders, possible consequences, uncertainty and vulnerability. Relevant scenarios should inform preparedness exercises, priorities and risk communication. Strategic level: Crisis During a crisis, the strategic objective is to limit harm and consequences. Communication is more than message distribution. It is an exchange of knowledge intended to reduce uncertainty, support coordinated action and limit secondary harm. Crisis managers must continue to identify problems that could generate new crises. The triggering event is not always what causes the most serious long-term consequences. Organisational conduct, unmet expectations or poor coordination can prolong and intensify the crisis. The PRK framework is based on teaching developed by Kristian Fuglseth at Volda University College, NTNU and HAW Kiel, and on experience from crisis exercises and municipal preparedness research. The SOFT analytical lens. The five fields supplement technical risk assessment; they do not replace it. The accompanying text defines each field. Questions for analysis Whose situation? Which groups carry the consequences, and which voices are missing from the organisation's picture? Whose expectations? What do different stakeholders consider reasonable, legitimate or safe? Whose frame? How do language, images, sources and categories define the matter? Which capacity? Can the organisation listen, coordinate, explain uncertainty and change established practice? Connect SOFT to the wider process Place the matter with PRK Use PRK to examine movement between a contested problem, risk and crisis. Open the PRK framework → Turn insight into work with FIVER Use FIVER to revise the situation analysis and organise an accountable response. Open the FIVER model → Full teaching text SOFT as a critical analytical lens Technical risk assessment cannot by itself explain how an issue becomes socially important. SOFT supplements probability and consequence analysis by examining social conditions, opinions, framing, transparency and organisational conditions. Social conditions Analysis starts with the conditions under which people encounter the issue. Exposure, resources, language, access, dependency and vulnerability are unevenly distributed. The same event may therefore have very different consequences for different groups. Opinions and expectations Stakeholder opinions are not substitutes for evidence. They can, however, reveal contested values, unmet expectations and emerging conflicts. Organisations must distinguish between disagreement about facts, disagreement about values and disagreement about what constitutes a legitimate response. Framing Frames select aspects of a matter and connect them to causes, consequences, responsibility and possible solutions. Analysis must ask which frame dominates, whose knowledge supports it and which alternatives remain less visible. Transparency and organisational conditions An organisation's ability to act and communicate depends on authority, information flows, professional culture, resources and coordination. Transparency requires more than publishing information. The organisation must explain uncertainty, identify limitations and show what it is prepared to change. SOFT is used as an author-developed teaching approach in risk, crisis and issue communication. The resource draws on teaching at Volda University College, NTNU and HAW Kiel, crisis exercises and municipal research.
